title: the mountain ahead
hook: back to the battlefield: a warrior drops his bow, and the conversation begins
carry: you have the right to act. Not to the fruit

segments.voice: Yesterday, satsang. Your line was good company changes you. Now, the whole camp, quickly: Ganesha, om, Gayatri, namaste, arti, ishta devata, karma, puja, dharma, atman, Brahman, guru, japa, shanti, seva, bhakti, ahimsa, maya, moksha, satsang. Twenty words. Today makes twenty-one. Day twenty-one.
screen: `GOOD COMPANY CHANGES YOU.` → the strand, twenty words lit.

segments.voice: Go back to day nine. A battlefield, two armies drawn up, conch shells blowing. Arjuna, a great archer, asks his charioteer to drive him out between the lines so he can see who he's about to fight. He looks across and sees teachers, uncles, cousins, friends. His mouth goes dry. His bow slips from his hand. And he sits down in the chariot and says he will not fight. We left him there, with his driver, Krishna, beside him. Today we find out what happens next. Because the whole conversation that follows has a name, and it's the last word of this camp.
screen: `BACK TO THE BATTLEFIELD.` → `HIS BOW SLIPS.` → `WHAT DOES THE DRIVER SAY?`

segments.voice: The Bhagavad Gita. The Song of the Lord. It sits inside the great epic, the Mahabharata, and it's a conversation between two people in a chariot. On day nine you heard that the driver is Krishna, and a great deal more than a driver. Krishna does more than give orders. He teaches. He talks about the self that cannot be killed, which you met as atman. He talks about acting without grabbing, about loving God, about seeing clearly. Look back at this week and you'll hear echoes. Action with the self out of the way, the way seva works. Love as a path of its own, bhakti. The Gita holds these paths side by side. Then the line this camp saved for last. In the second chapter Krishna says, in plain words: your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting. And the verse keeps going: don't let that become a reason to do nothing, either. It isn't a way out of the fight. It's a way to stand up and act without being owned by the result. And near the end of the Gita comes a surprise. After everything, Krishna tells Arjuna to think it over fully, and then do as he chooses. He hands the choice back. In the fourth camp you'll read this text itself, line by line. For now you get the door, and the sentence that opens it.
screen: `THE SONG OF THE LORD, IN A CHARIOT.` · `THE WHOLE CAMP IS IN THERE.` · `NOT A WAY OUT. A WAY TO STAND UP.` · `THINK IT OVER. THEN CHOOSE.` · then, large: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick up the bow. Sit and breathe. Press your palms together at your chest, the way you did on day one. Bring to mind one thing that's yours to do this week, the thing you've been sitting down in the chariot about. Picture doing it, fully. Then open your hand, and let go of how it turns out. The action is yours. The fruit isn't. If you pray, you can offer the result to God. The bell holds the time.
The Gita. The Song of the Lord, a conversation in a chariot that gets a warrior back on his feet. Twenty-first word, and the door to the mountain.
screen: `THE GITA — your 21st word` → the strand complete → `CAMP 1. FIRST WORDS. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: you have the right to act. Not to the fruit. Do one thing today that's yours to do, and let the result go. Tomorrow the stories begin, with a goddess, a bath, and a boy made of earth. Day twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 21 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOY AT THE DOOR.`

howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and some memorize its verses; its teaching on action without attachment to results is quoted in daily life.

fork.setup: you're Krishna. your friend Arjuna has dropped his bow and says he won't fight. you've taught him everything. near the end, what do you tell him?
options: tell him to think it over fully, then choose.
fork.reveal: near the end he hands the choice back: reflect on all of it, then do as you choose.

original.note: Sanskrit: the song (gita) of the Lord (bhagavat).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita is a book of rules.
what it means: a conversation in a chariot that gets a man back on his feet. act fully; let go of the fruit.
what a scholar hears: Gita 2.47, your right is to action alone, never to its fruits, and don't cling to inaction; and 18.63, reflect fully, then do as you wish.
